questions.q: The four classic millennial views are distinguished chiefly by how they relate which two things?
options: The date of Revelation and the identity of the beast
The number of resurrections and the location of heaven
The timing of Christ's return and the nature of the thousand years of Revelation 20
The order of the Gospels and the authorship of Revelation
questions.explanation: Premillennialists place the Second Coming before the millennium, postmillennialists after it, and amillennialists read the thousand years of Revelation 20:1-6 as the present age, so 'no future millennium' rather than 'no millennium'.

questions.q: Why does this study treat preterism, historicism, futurism and idealism separately from the millennial views?
options: They are approaches to the timing and reference of Revelation's prophecies, and can combine with more than one millennial view
They are four older names for the four millennial views
They are Roman Catholic alternatives to Protestant millennial views
They concern only the book of Daniel, not Revelation
questions.explanation: The hermeneutic approaches ask when and to what Revelation's visions refer; for example, partial preterism pairs with postmillennialism (Gentry, Mathison) and with amillennialism, and futurism pairs with both kinds of premillennialism.

questions.q: What do the ecumenical creeds affirm about the end that all the historic millennial views share?
options: A literal thousand-year reign on earth after Christ's return
A pretribulational rapture of the church
That the millennium began in AD 70
Christ will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, with the resurrection of the dead
questions.explanation: The Apostles' and Nicene Creeds confess Christ's return to judge and the resurrection, but take no position on the millennium; the millennial debate takes place inside that shared creedal core.

questions.q: Which 1977 multi-view book, edited by Robert G. Clouse, set the modern pattern of comparing millennial views side by side?
options: Revelation: Four Views
The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views
Three Views on the Rapture
When Shall These Things Be?
questions.explanation: Clouse's volume had George Eldon Ladd (historic premillennialism), Herman Hoyt (dispensational premillennialism), Loraine Boettner (postmillennialism) and Anthony Hoekema (amillennialism) present and respond to each other.

questions.q: The phrase 'already and not yet', associated with Geerhardus Vos, Oscar Cullmann and George Ladd, means that
options: The rapture has already happened for some believers but not for others
The kingdom and the age to come have broken in with Christ's first coming but await consummation at his return
Some prophecies were fulfilled in AD 70 and none remain
The millennium has begun in heaven but will never come on earth
questions.explanation: Inaugurated eschatology holds that the 'last days' began with Christ's resurrection and Pentecost (Acts 2:16-17; Hebrews 1:2) while the resurrection of the body and new creation remain future. Nearly every modern view uses some version of it.

questions.q: Why is Matthew 24:34 ('this generation will not pass away') so central to the debate?
options: It is the only verse that mentions the millennium
It is missing from the oldest manuscripts
It names the Antichrist
Its time reference shapes whether the Olivet Discourse is read as fulfilled in AD 70, still future, or both
questions.explanation: Preterists take 'this generation' as Jesus' contemporaries and see fulfilment in Jerusalem's fall; many futurists read it as 'the generation that sees these signs' or 'this race'; others divide the discourse between AD 70 and the final coming.

questions.q: Which statement about the date of Revelation is accurate?
options: It is disputed: most scholars favour c. AD 95 under Domitian, while a significant minority argue for a date before AD 70
All scholars agree it was written in AD 68
It was certainly written after AD 135
The book itself states the year of writing
questions.explanation: The late date rests heavily on Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3); early-date advocates such as Gentry (Before Jerusalem Fell) and J. A. T. Robinson appeal to internal evidence like the temple in Revelation 11:1-2. The question matters most for preterist readings.

questions.q: Daniel 9:24-27 (the 'seventy weeks') is a flashpoint mainly because interpreters disagree about
options: Whether Daniel was written in Greek or Aramaic
Whether the weeks are counted from the Exodus
Whether the seventieth week followed the sixty-ninth directly in Christ's ministry or is separated from it by a gap reaching to the end of the age
Whether the passage mentions the Messiah at all
questions.explanation: Dispensationalists see a gap with a future seven-year week (the tribulation); many covenant interpreters see the week fulfilled in Christ's death and the following years, with Jerusalem's destruction as its consequence.

questions.q: What is 'chiliasm'?
options: The belief that the world will end in the year 1000
A Latin term for the binding of Satan
The Reformed doctrine of the covenant of works
An older name, from the Greek for 'thousand', for belief in a future earthly millennial reign of Christ
questions.explanation: Chiliasm (Greek chilioi, 'thousand'; Latin equivalent millenarianism) describes the premillennial expectation held by early writers such as Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus.

questions.q: Where does the word 'rapture' come from?
options: The Latin rapiemur ('we shall be caught up') in the Vulgate of 1 Thessalonians 4:17
The Hebrew word for 'trumpet' in Joel 2
A nineteenth-century coinage by C. I. Scofield
The Greek title of the book of Revelation
questions.explanation: All views believe believers will be 'caught up' to meet the Lord (Greek harpazo). The dispute is over timing: pretribulational, midtribulational, prewrath, posttribulational, or simultaneous with a single final return.

questions.q: What does postmillennialism hold about the relation of Christ's return to the millennium?
options: Christ returns before a literal thousand-year reign in Jerusalem
There is no millennium at all, present or future
Christ returns after a long era in which the gospel, through the Spirit, brings the great majority of people and nations to faith
Christ returned spiritually in AD 70 and there is no future coming
questions.explanation: Postmillennialists such as Loraine Boettner (The Millennium, 1957) and Kenneth Gentry (He Shall Have Dominion) teach that Christ's kingdom grows through gospel means, issuing in a 'golden age' before a single, visible Second Coming, general resurrection and judgment.

questions.q: Which parables do postmillennialists commonly cite for the gradual, pervasive growth of the kingdom?
options: The ten virgins and the talents (Matthew 25)
The mustard seed and the leaven (Matthew 13:31-33)
The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31)
The prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32)
questions.explanation: The kingdom begins small but grows to fill the field and permeate the whole lump; postmillennialists combine these with Daniel 2:35, where the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth.

questions.q: How do postmillennialists use Psalm 110:1 together with 1 Corinthians 15:24-26?
options: They argue Christ will begin to reign only after he returns
They read both texts as fulfilled in Solomon
Christ reigns now from heaven until his enemies are made his footstool, so his return comes at the end of that conquering reign
They hold the enemies are subdued only in heaven, not on earth
questions.explanation: Psalm 110:1 is the Old Testament text most quoted in the New Testament; postmillennialists stress that Christ sits at the right hand 'until' his enemies are subdued, with death the last enemy destroyed at his coming.

questions.q: What role did Daniel Whitby (1638-1726) play in the history of postmillennialism?
options: His 'Treatise of the True Millennium' (1703) popularised a systematic postmillennial scheme, though optimistic views predate him
He founded dispensationalism at Powerscourt
He wrote the Westminster Confession's chapter on the last things
He was the first to teach that the Pope is Antichrist
questions.explanation: Critics sometimes call Whitby the 'founder' of postmillennialism; proponents such as Iain Murray (The Puritan Hope) document that Puritans like Thomas Brightman, John Owen and others held hopes of a latter-day spread of the gospel well before him.

questions.q: Why do postmillennialists often cite the Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 191?
options: It explicitly defines a thousand-year golden age before Christ's return
It condemns premillennialism by name
It dates Revelation before AD 70
Its exposition of 'Thy kingdom come' asks that the gospel be spread through the world, the Jews called, and the fullness of the Gentiles brought in
questions.explanation: The catechism does not adopt a millennial scheme, so the link is an inference; postmillennialists argue that the prayer it teaches expects a worldwide gospel triumph and a future conversion of Israel (Romans 11:25-26).

questions.q: Which of these figures is a historic representative of postmillennialism?
options: John Nelson Darby
Jonathan Edwards
Anthony Hoekema
George Eldon Ladd
questions.explanation: Edwards, the Princeton theologians Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield, and many nineteenth-century American evangelicals held postmillennial hopes; Darby was a dispensationalist, Hoekema an amillennialist, Ladd a historic premillennialist.

questions.q: What is commonly given as a reason postmillennialism declined in the early twentieth century?
options: Its rejection by the Westminster Assembly
The shock of the world wars and its perceived association with the liberal 'social gospel'
The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls
Its condemnation at the Council of Ephesus
questions.explanation: Postmillennialists respond that their hope rests on the Spirit's work through the gospel rather than on human progress, and that evangelical postmillennialism differs fundamentally from social-gospel optimism; the view revived from the 1970s through writers such as Rushdoony, Bahnsen, Gentry and Mathison.

questions.q: Contemporary postmillennialism is often divided into two broad streams. Which pair is correct?
options: Pretribulational and posttribulational postmillennialism
Historic and progressive postmillennialism
Jewish and Gentile postmillennialism
Revivalist (Puritan/Edwardsean) postmillennialism and theonomic or Reconstructionist postmillennialism
questions.explanation: Iain Murray and Keith Mathison represent a revival-centred emphasis, while R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen and Gentry linked postmillennial hope with the application of biblical law to society; many postmillennialists hold neither theonomy nor its rejection as essential.

questions.q: How did B. B. Warfield interpret Revelation 20:1-10 in 'The Millennium and the Apocalypse' (1904)?
options: As a vision of the blessed state of saints in heaven during the present age, while he located postmillennial hope in other texts
As a literal thousand years after a future rapture
As fulfilled entirely in the reign of Constantine
As a prediction of the Protestant Reformation
questions.explanation: Warfield's reading of Revelation 20 resembles amillennial exegesis; his optimism about the gospel's worldwide victory came from texts such as 1 Corinthians 15 and from Revelation 19's picture of the conquering Word.

questions.q: How do postmillennialists usually answer the objection that 2 Timothy 3:1-5 and Luke 18:8 predict worsening conditions?
options: They deny these books are canonical
They agree the world will grow steadily worse until Christ returns
Many read these as describing particular periods (such as the apostolic generation) or as compatible with overall progress that includes setbacks
They apply these verses only to the millennium after Christ returns
questions.explanation: Gentry and others argue the 'last days' language often refers to the era beginning with Christ's first coming, and that persecution and apostasy coexist with the long-term advance of the kingdom, as in the parable of the wheat and tares.

questions.q: What does amillennialism hold about the thousand years of Revelation 20?
options: They are a literal future era after Christ returns
They never refer to any real period
They ended in AD 70 and nothing has followed
They symbolise the present age between Christ's first and second comings, during which Christ reigns and the saints reign with him
questions.explanation: Anthony Hoekema (The Bible and the Future) and Kim Riddlebarger (A Case for Amillennialism) stress that amillennialists affirm a millennium; they deny only a future earthly one.

questions.q: Which term did Jay E. Adams propose (in a 1959 book later reissued as 'The Time Is at Hand') as a better name than 'amillennialism'?
options: Realized millennialism
Inaugurated chiliasm
Progressive covenantalism
Covenant eschatology
questions.explanation: Adams argued the prefix 'a-' wrongly suggests no millennium; 'realized' signals that the millennium is being realized now. Hoekema likewise noted the term 'amillennialism' is unfortunate.

questions.q: How do amillennialists interpret the binding of Satan in Revelation 20:2-3?
options: Satan is entirely inactive during the present age
Satan will be bound only after a future seven-year tribulation
It is a restriction on Satan's ability to deceive the nations and prevent the gospel's spread, accomplished by Christ's first coming
The binding is a metaphor for the end of the Roman Empire
questions.explanation: They link it to Matthew 12:29 (binding the strong man), Luke 10:18 and John 12:31-32: the nations, once deceived, can now be reached by the gospel even though Satan still prowls (1 Peter 5:8).

questions.q: Amillennialists commonly identify the 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:5-6 as
options: The bodily resurrection of believers at a pretribulational rapture
A spiritual reality: either regeneration or, more commonly today, believers' entry into Christ's presence at death
The rebuilding of the temple
The conversion of Israel at the end of the age
questions.explanation: Hoekema and Meredith Kline read the scene as the souls of martyrs living and reigning in heaven (Revelation 20:4); premillennialists reply that 'came to life' (ezesan) should mean bodily resurrection in both verses 4 and 5.

questions.q: Which early theologian's 'City of God' (Book 20) shaped the dominant amillennial reading in the Western church?
options: Justin Martyr
Irenaeus of Lyons
Augustine of Hippo
Papias of Hierapolis
questions.explanation: Augustine, who had earlier held a form of chiliasm, came to read the thousand years as the church age, building on the Donatist exegete Tyconius; Justin, Irenaeus and Papias were premillennial.

questions.q: What is 'progressive parallelism' (recapitulation), which many amillennialists apply to Revelation?
options: The view that Revelation's sections repeatedly cover the whole period between the comings from different angles
The view that Revelation 4-22 is in strict chronological order
The idea that each church in Revelation 2-3 represents a future era
The belief that Revelation repeats Daniel word for word
questions.explanation: William Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors identified seven parallel sections; on this reading Revelation 20:1 begins again at the first coming rather than following 19:11-21 chronologically.

questions.q: Which texts do amillennialists cite for a single general resurrection and judgment at Christ's return?
options: Revelation 20:4-6 alone
Daniel 9:27 and Ezekiel 40-48
Zechariah 14:4 and Isaiah 65:20
John 5:28-29 and Matthew 25:31-46
questions.explanation: Jesus speaks of one 'hour' when all in the tombs come out, some to life and some to judgment, and of a single gathering of the nations; amillennialists see no room for a thousand-year interval between the resurrections.

questions.q: The 'two-age' structure emphasised by Geerhardus Vos and Kim Riddlebarger holds that
options: There are two separate peoples of God with two destinies
Scripture contrasts 'this age' and 'the age to come', with the age to come beginning at Christ's return in resurrection and new creation
History is divided into the age of law and the age of grace
The millennium is a third age between this age and the age to come
questions.explanation: Texts such as Luke 20:34-36 and Matthew 12:32 put resurrection and the age to come together; amillennialists argue this leaves no slot for a further earthly age after the Second Coming.

questions.q: How does amillennialism usually regard the course of history before Christ's return?
options: The world will be almost entirely Christianised
The kingdom grows alongside evil, with suffering and gospel advance both continuing until the end; views range from cautious to optimistic
The church will be removed before a seven-year tribulation
Nothing of significance happens between the comings
questions.explanation: The wheat and tares grow together until harvest (Matthew 13:24-30); some amillennialists stress a final apostasy, while others (sometimes called 'optimistic amillennialists') stress gospel growth.

questions.q: Which Reformation-era confession explicitly rejected the idea of an earthly reign of the saints before the resurrection?
options: The Westminster Larger Catechism
The Scofield Reference Bible
The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
The Augsburg Confession (Article 17)
questions.explanation: Article 17 condemns those spreading 'Jewish opinions' of a worldly kingdom of the godly before the resurrection; the Second Helvetic Confession has a similar rejection. Premillennialists note these were aimed largely at radical Anabaptist movements.

questions.q: What is the central claim of historic premillennialism?
options: Christ returns once, after the tribulation, raises believers, and then reigns on earth for a millennium before the final judgment
Christ returns twice: secretly for the church and later with it
The millennium is the present church age
The millennium is a golden age before Christ returns
questions.explanation: George Eldon Ladd (The Blessed Hope, 1956) defended a single posttribulational return followed by a millennial reign, without dispensationalism's sharp Israel-church distinction.

questions.q: Why is the view called 'historic' premillennialism?
options: It was the official view of the Council of Nicaea
It was invented by historians in the nineteenth century
Proponents argue it resembles the chiliasm of second-century writers such as Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus
It interprets Revelation by the day-year principle
questions.explanation: Justin's Dialogue with Trypho (80-81) and Irenaeus's Against Heresies Book 5 expected a future reign in a restored Jerusalem; Justin also admitted that some orthodox Christians thought otherwise.

questions.q: What exegetical argument about Revelation 20:4-5 do historic premillennialists consider decisive?
options: The word 'thousand' never means a literal number in Greek
The first resurrection refers to Israel's national restoration
The verses are missing from early manuscripts
The same verb, 'came to life' (ezesan), should mean bodily resurrection in both verses, so there are two bodily resurrections separated by the thousand years
questions.explanation: Henry Alford famously argued that if the second resurrection is literal the first must be too; Ladd and Craig Blomberg repeat the point. Amillennialists reply that John contrasts a spiritual first resurrection with physical death.

questions.q: How do historic premillennialists read 1 Corinthians 15:23-24?
options: As a sequence (Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at his coming, then the end) that leaves room for an interval before the end
As proof that there will be no future resurrection
As fulfilled entirely at Pentecost
As describing a secret rapture before the tribulation
questions.explanation: The words 'then' (epeita, eita) can mark intervals, as between Christ's resurrection and his coming; Ladd suggested the millennium falls between 'at his coming' and 'the end'. Critics answer that 'the end' follows the coming directly.

questions.q: What view of the rapture do most historic premillennialists hold?
options: Pretribulational: the church is removed seven years before Christ returns
Partial rapture: only watchful believers are taken
Posttribulational: the church goes through the tribulation and is caught up to meet Christ as he comes
No rapture of any kind
questions.explanation: Douglas Moo argued the posttribulational view in Three Views on the Rapture (1984), and Robert Gundry's The Church and the Tribulation (1973) is a classic statement; Alan Kurschner's prewrath view is a related variant.

questions.q: How does George Ladd's understanding of the kingdom of God differ from classic dispensationalism?
options: He believed the kingdom was offered to Israel and withdrawn until the end
He saw the kingdom as God's reign already inaugurated in Jesus' ministry, not wholly postponed until the millennium
He identified the kingdom with the visible church on earth
He denied that the kingdom has any future aspect
questions.explanation: Ladd's The Gospel of the Kingdom and A Theology of the New Testament popularised the 'already and not yet' framework among evangelicals; the millennium is a future stage of a kingdom already present.

questions.q: How do historic premillennialists typically see the relation of Israel and the church?
options: Two peoples with permanently separate destinies and programmes
The church has no connection to Old Testament promises
One people of God, while many still expect a future large-scale turning of ethnic Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25-26)
Israel will be saved apart from faith in Christ
questions.explanation: This continuity is a key difference from dispensationalism; contributors to A Case for Historic Premillennialism (Blomberg and Chung, eds., 2009) argue the case from Scripture and church history.

questions.q: What purpose do historic premillennialists often give for a millennial reign after Christ's return?
options: It displays Christ's public victory within history and vindicates God's purposes for the created order before the final state
It allows unbelievers a second chance after the final judgment
It replaces the new heavens and new earth
It exists to rebuild the temple sacrifices for atonement
questions.explanation: Proponents such as Ladd and Wayne Grudem argue the reign shows that the curse is partially lifted and Christ's rule is vindicated on earth; critics ask why glorified saints would share the world with mortals.

questions.q: What is a common amillennial objection to historic premillennialism, and the typical reply?
options: That it denies the Second Coming; they reply it affirms two comings
That it requires a pre-AD 70 date for Revelation; they reply with Irenaeus
That it rejects Romans 11; they reply by rejecting Romans
That Revelation 20 is the only text teaching an interim kingdom; premillennialists reply that one clear text suffices and that other texts allow for it
questions.explanation: Critics stress that no other passage explicitly mentions a thousand-year reign after the parousia; premillennialists answer that Isaiah 65:20, Zechariah 14 and 1 Corinthians 15 fit such an interval and that Scripture need only say something once.

questions.q: Which sequence best summarises dispensational premillennialism?
options: Gospel growth, golden age, Christ's return, final judgment
Pretribulational rapture, seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week), Christ's return, a literal thousand-year reign centred on Israel
Church age, single return, general resurrection, new creation
AD 70 parousia, eternal kingdom, no further return
questions.explanation: Classic statements include J. Dwight Pentecost's Things to Come (1958) and John Walvoord's The Rapture Question (1957) and The Millennial Kingdom.

questions.q: Which figure, associated with the Plymouth Brethren and the Powerscourt conferences in Ireland (1831-1833), systematised dispensational teaching?
options: Jonathan Edwards
John Nelson Darby
Francisco Ribera
Daniel Whitby
questions.explanation: Lady Theodosia Powerscourt hosted prophecy conferences at her Wicklow estate, where Darby developed his distinction between Israel and the church and a pretribulational 'catching up' of the church.

questions.q: What made the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) so influential?
options: It was the first English translation of the Bible
It was the official Bible of the Church of England
It introduced the day-year principle
Its notes carried dispensational premillennialism into a widely used study Bible across English-speaking evangelicalism
questions.explanation: C. I. Scofield's notes (Oxford University Press; revised 1917 and 1967) divided history into seven dispensations and taught a pretribulational rapture; Dallas Theological Seminary (founded 1924 by Lewis Sperry Chafer) carried the tradition forward.

questions.q: How do dispensationalists read Daniel 9:26-27?
options: The seventieth week is separated from the sixty-ninth by the church age and will be fulfilled in a future seven-year tribulation
The seventieth week ended at the crucifixion with no gap
The seventy weeks are symbolic of the whole of world history
The passage refers only to Antiochus Epiphanes
questions.explanation: The 'he' who confirms a covenant (Daniel 9:27) is read as the coming Antichrist; critics argue the text gives no gap and that 'he' is Messiah, while dispensationalists point to prophetic gaps elsewhere (e.g. Isaiah 61:1-2 in Luke 4:18-19).

questions.q: Which text is the primary description of the rapture for dispensationalists?
options: Revelation 20:1-3
Matthew 13:31-33
1 Thessalonians 4:13-18
Daniel 2:44
questions.explanation: All views accept the 'catching up' of 1 Thessalonians 4:17; pretribulationists add arguments from promises of deliverance from wrath (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 5:9; Revelation 3:10) and from the church's absence from Revelation 4-19.

questions.q: Why is 'imminence' important to the pretribulational argument?
options: It shows the rapture happened in AD 70
It proves the millennium is the present age
It means Christ will return in the year 2000
If Christ may come for the church at any moment with no signs preceding, the rapture must precede the tribulation events
questions.explanation: Walvoord and Thomas Ice argue that New Testament exhortations to watch (e.g. James 5:8-9; Titus 2:13) imply no prophesied event must come first; posttribulationists reply that watching is compatible with expected signs (Matthew 24:33).

questions.q: What role does national Israel have in the dispensational millennium?
options: Israel is restored to its land and receives the fulfilment of its covenant promises, with Christ reigning from Jerusalem
Israel plays no distinct role, having been replaced by the church
Israel is judged and excluded
Israel's promises were fulfilled in the Maccabean era
questions.explanation: Dispensationalists read the Abrahamic, Davidic and new covenant promises (e.g. Genesis 15; 2 Samuel 7; Jeremiah 31; Ezekiel 40-48) as including a literal national and territorial fulfilment.

questions.q: Which of these rapture views is held by some premillennialists but is NOT the classic dispensational position?
options: The pretribulational view
The view that the rapture precedes Daniel's seventieth week
The prewrath view (rapture during the second half of the seventieth week, before God's wrath)
The view that the church is absent from Revelation 4-19
questions.explanation: Marvin Rosenthal and Alan Kurschner developed the prewrath view; Gleason Archer argued a mid-seventieth-week rapture in Three Views on the Rapture (1984). Classic dispensationalism is pretribulational.

questions.q: How does progressive dispensationalism (Blaising, Bock, Saucy, early 1990s) differ from earlier forms?
options: It abandons premillennialism for amillennialism
It sees more continuity, holding that Christ is already reigning in an inaugurated Davidic kingdom while still expecting a future for national Israel
It rejects any distinction between Israel and the church
It teaches that the rapture happened in AD 70
questions.explanation: Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock's Progressive Dispensationalism (1993) and Robert Saucy's The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism (1993) present an 'already/not yet' Davidic reign; most remain pretribulational but some are less committed to it.

questions.q: What does partial preterism hold?
options: Every prophecy, including the resurrection, was fulfilled by AD 70
No prophecy has yet been fulfilled
Many prophecies, including much of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation, were fulfilled in the events of AD 66-70, while the Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment remain future
Revelation outlines church history from Pentecost to the present
questions.explanation: R. C. Sproul's The Last Days According to Jesus (1998), Kenneth Gentry and Gary DeMar defend this view; 'preterist' comes from Latin praeteritus, 'gone by'.

questions.q: Which 'time texts' are central to partial preterist arguments?
options: Matthew 24:34, Matthew 16:28 and Revelation 1:1, 3 ('the time is near')
Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1
Daniel 12:2 and Revelation 20:12
Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8
questions.explanation: Preterists argue that 'this generation', 'some standing here' and 'what must soon take place' signal fulfilment within the first readers' lifetime; futurists reply that these may express certainty, prophetic perspective, or a future generation.

questions.q: Which Counter-Reformation Jesuit is often credited with the first systematic preterist commentary on Revelation?
options: Francisco Ribera
Manuel Lacunza
Robert Bellarmine
Luis de Alcázar (Vestigatio arcani sensus in Apocalypsi, 1614)
questions.explanation: Alcázar read most of Revelation as fulfilled in the church's victories over Judaism and pagan Rome; Ribera's commentary pointed in the opposite, futurist direction. Earlier writers such as Eusebius also saw parts of the Olivet Discourse fulfilled in AD 70.

questions.q: How does Gentry identify the beast's number 666 (Revelation 13:18)?
options: The Pope, through the Latin title Vicarius Filii Dei
Nero Caesar, whose name in Hebrew letters (Nrwn Qsr) totals 666
Muhammad
A future world ruler who has not yet appeared
questions.explanation: Gentry also notes the variant reading 616, which matches the Latin spelling Nero Caesar, as supporting evidence; critics question whether Asian Gentile readers would compute a Hebrew spelling.

questions.q: Why does the dating of Revelation matter so much for partial preterism?
options: Because a late date would prove dispensationalism
If Revelation was written before AD 70, its 'soon' prophecies can refer to the Jewish War; a c. AD 95 date makes AD 70 fulfilment of Revelation impossible
Because the date determines the author's identity
Because a pre-70 date would place Revelation before the Gospels in every case
questions.explanation: Gentry's Before Jerusalem Fell argues for c. AD 65-66 from internal evidence such as the temple (Revelation 11:1-2) and the sixth king (17:10). Most scholars still favour the Domitianic date, so the question is disputed. Some preterists apply Revelation to Rome's fall instead.

questions.q: How do partial preterists read 'the Son of Man coming on the clouds' in Matthew 24:30?
options: As the bodily Second Coming at the end of history only
As the pretribulational rapture
As a reference to Pentecost
As a judgment-coming against Jerusalem, echoing Old Testament cloud-comings of God in judgment (e.g. Isaiah 19:1) and Daniel 7:13's enthronement
questions.explanation: N. T. Wright and Gentry read Daniel 7:13 as the Son of Man's vindication before the Ancient of Days. Many partial preterists then see a transition to the final coming at Matthew 24:36 or later.

questions.q: Which ancient historian do partial preterists cite most often for the details of Jerusalem's fall?
options: Josephus (The Jewish War)
Herodotus
Thucydides
Bede
questions.explanation: Josephus describes famine, false prophets, the siege and the temple's burning, which preterists match with Matthew 24 and Luke 21:20-24. Critics caution against reading Josephus's rhetoric too precisely.

questions.q: What is the key difference between partial and full preterism?
options: Partial preterists date Revelation after AD 95
Full preterists deny that AD 70 had any prophetic significance
Partial preterists affirm a future bodily Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment; full preterists place all of these in the first century
Partial preterists reject the creeds
questions.explanation: Partial preterists often cite Acts 1:11 and 1 Corinthians 15 for a future visible return and bodily resurrection, and several (e.g. Mathison's edited volume When Shall These Things Be?) have written critiques of full preterism.

questions.q: With which millennial views is partial preterism commonly combined?
options: Only dispensational premillennialism
Only historicist premillennialism
None; it rejects all millennial views
Postmillennialism and amillennialism
questions.explanation: Gentry and DeMar are postmillennial; many amillennialists, and Sproul (who did not commit firmly), accept preterist readings of the Olivet Discourse. The pairing with dispensational premillennialism is rare because dispensationalists place these prophecies in a future tribulation.

questions.q: What does full preterism (also called 'consistent' or 'covenant eschatology') hold?
options: All biblical prophecy, including the Second Coming, resurrection and final judgment, was fulfilled by AD 70
The Second Coming is future but the tribulation is past
Revelation describes church history to the present
Most prophecy remains future
questions.explanation: Advocates such as Max King (The Spirit of Prophecy, 1971; The Cross and the Parousia of Christ, 1987) and Don Preston argue that the time texts require a complete first-century fulfilment.

questions.q: Why do critics say full preterism stands outside historic creedal orthodoxy?
options: It rejects the Trinity
It denies Christ's bodily resurrection on the third day
The ecumenical creeds confess a future return of Christ to judge and a future resurrection of the body, which full preterism places in the past
It teaches a pretribulational rapture
questions.explanation: Critics such as Keith Mathison (ed., When Shall These Things Be?, 2004) argue this; proponents respond that creeds are subordinate to Scripture and that they affirm the return and resurrection as biblical events, though now fulfilled. Most full preterists affirm the Trinity and Christ's own bodily resurrection.

questions.q: Which nineteenth-century book is often regarded as a precursor of modern full preterism?
options: Darby's Synopsis of the Books of the Bible
J. Stuart Russell's The Parousia (1878)
Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae
Hendriksen's More Than Conquerors
questions.explanation: Russell, a Congregationalist minister, argued that every New Testament reference to the parousia pointed to the destruction of Jerusalem; the work was reprinted and became influential among later full preterists.

questions.q: How do many full preterists, following Max King, understand the resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15?
options: As the resurrection of all bodies from their graves at a future date
As reincarnation
As a corporate, covenantal resurrection of the people of God from the old covenant into the new, completed in AD 70
As fulfilled only in the conversion of individual believers today
questions.explanation: Some full preterists instead hold an individual view in which believers receive immortal bodies in heaven at death. Critics point to the bodily resurrection of Christ as 'firstfruits' (1 Corinthians 15:20-23) as requiring a like resurrection of believers' bodies.

questions.q: Which text do critics cite as an apostolic warning relevant to full preterism?
options: 2 Timothy 2:17-18, on Hymenaeus and Philetus saying the resurrection had already happened
Romans 11:25-26
Revelation 1:7
questions.explanation: Critics see a parallel with claiming a past resurrection; full preterists reply that the error lay in claiming completion before AD 70, not in claiming the resurrection would occur within that generation.

questions.q: What is the core argument full preterists press against partial preterists?
options: That Revelation was written after AD 95
That the Gospels are unreliable
That the Olivet Discourse refers only to the end of the world
If the time texts limit the 'coming' in Matthew 24 to that generation, the same consistency should apply to other coming and resurrection texts
questions.explanation: Full preterists argue that the Olivet Discourse is a single coming and that texts like Matthew 16:27-28 tie judgment to Jesus' generation. Partial preterists respond that Scripture speaks of more than one 'coming', and that texts like Acts 1:11 describe a visible, bodily return.

questions.q: Which passage do critics stress as requiring a future, visible, bodily return?
options: Matthew 13:33
Acts 1:11 (Jesus will come 'in the same way' as he was seen going into heaven)
Psalm 2:8
Daniel 9:25
questions.explanation: Critics argue 'in the same way' implies a bodily, visible return; full preterists typically read it as a cloud-coming in judgment, comparable to Old Testament theophanies.

questions.q: What do full preterists say about history after AD 70?
options: The world will end in a future tribulation
The kingdom is fully established and continues indefinitely, with the church living in the new covenant age without a future end-of-history event
History ended in AD 70 and nothing since is real
A future rapture is still expected
questions.explanation: Most full preterists hold that human history continues without end and that believers enter heaven at death; critics see this as removing the Christian hope of bodily resurrection and new creation (Romans 8:18-23).

questions.q: What does historicism hold about the book of Revelation?
options: It was entirely fulfilled by AD 70
It describes only the final seven years before Christ returns
It conveys timeless principles with no specific historical referents
It forecasts the course of church and world history from the apostolic age to Christ's return in sequence
questions.explanation: Historicists read the seals, trumpets and bowls as successive eras of history; it was the dominant Protestant approach from the Reformation to the mid-nineteenth century.

questions.q: What is the 'day-year principle'?
options: Prophetic days stand for years, so 1,260 days (Revelation 12:6) signify 1,260 years
Each day of creation lasted a thousand years
A day with the Lord is as a thousand years, so the millennium is a single day
Prophecies about days must be fulfilled within one year
questions.explanation: Historicists appeal to Numbers 14:34 and Ezekiel 4:6, and to the seventy 'weeks' of Daniel 9 being weeks of years; critics argue these texts are specific instances rather than a general rule.

questions.q: Whom did the Protestant Reformers and most historicists identify as the Antichrist or man of lawlessness?
options: Nero
A future Jewish world ruler
The papacy, understood as an office rather than a single individual
The Ottoman sultan alone
questions.explanation: Luther, Calvin and many later Protestants held this; the original Westminster Confession (25.6) called the pope 'that Antichrist', a line later removed by several Presbyterian bodies. Many historicists also identified Islam with parts of the trumpet visions.

questions.q: Which pair are notable English historicist interpreters of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries?
options: John Nelson Darby and C. I. Scofield
Max King and Don Preston
William Hendriksen and Greg Beale
Joseph Mede and Isaac Newton
questions.explanation: Mede's Clavis Apocalyptica (1627) and Newton's Observations upon the Prophecies of Daniel and the Apocalypse of St. John (published 1733) shaped later historicism; Mede also revived premillennial expectation among English Puritans.

questions.q: Which nineteenth-century work is a monumental four-volume historicist commentary on Revelation?
options: E. B. Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae (1844)
Gentry's Before Jerusalem Fell
Pentecost's Things to Come
Wright's Jesus and the Victory of God
questions.explanation: Elliott interpreted Revelation as a detailed chronology of church history; Albert Barnes's Notes also followed a historicist approach in America.

questions.q: With which millennial views has historicism been combined?
options: Only dispensational premillennialism
Only full preterism
Both premillennialism and postmillennialism (and some amillennialism)
None; historicism has no view of the millennium
questions.explanation: Mede was premillennial, many Puritans and Jonathan Edwards combined historicist exegesis with postmillennial hope, and Seventh-day Adventism today combines historicism with its own distinctive millennial view.

questions.q: What is a common criticism of historicism, and how do historicists reply?
options: It ignores the Old Testament; they reply it uses only Daniel
Interpreters disagree widely and repeatedly identify their own era as the climax; historicists reply that the overall pattern of fulfilment is clear even if details are debated
It denies the Second Coming; they reply it is preterist
It requires a late date of Revelation; they reply with Gentry
questions.explanation: Failed date-setting (for example, around 1844) damaged the approach's credibility; defenders argue that the identification of the papacy and the rise of Islam display real prophetic fulfilment.

questions.q: Where is historicism still prominent today?
options: In dispensational seminaries such as Dallas
In the Roman Catholic magisterium
In Seventh-day Adventism and among some confessional Protestant writers
In all major evangelical study Bibles
questions.explanation: Adventist prophetic interpretation (e.g. LeRoy Froom's The Prophetic Faith of Our Fathers) is historicist, and some Reformed and Presbyterian writers continue the Reformation tradition.

questions.q: What does futurism hold about the book of Revelation?
options: Most of Revelation, typically chapters 4-22, describes events still future, clustered around Christ's return
Revelation was fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem
Revelation traces church history from the apostles to now
Revelation teaches only timeless principles
questions.explanation: Futurism is held by dispensationalists (Walvoord, The Revelation of Jesus Christ, 1966) and in modified forms by many historic premillennialists such as Ladd.

questions.q: What was Francisco Ribera's role in the history of futurism?
options: He invented the pretribulational rapture
He wrote the first preterist commentary
He founded the Plymouth Brethren
This Spanish Jesuit's commentary on Revelation (c. 1590) placed most of the book in a future period of three and a half years under a single Antichrist
questions.explanation: Ribera's work is widely seen as a Counter-Reformation response to the Protestant identification of the papacy with Antichrist; futurists note that early writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus already expected a future Antichrist.

questions.q: Who was Manuel Lacunza?
options: An Anglican bishop who devised the day-year principle
A Chilean Jesuit whose futurist premillennial work, published under the name 'Juan Josafat Ben-Ezra', was translated by Edward Irving in 1827
The editor of the Scofield Reference Bible
A Puritan who wrote the Savoy Declaration
questions.explanation: The Coming of Messiah in Glory and Majesty influenced the British prophetic movement of the 1820s and 1830s, including circles around Irving and the Albury and Powerscourt conferences.

questions.q: What do futurists claim about early church support?
options: The early church universally held the pretribulational rapture
Early writers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus expected a future personal Antichrist and future tribulation before Christ's return
The early church read Revelation as fulfilled in AD 70
The early church never commented on Revelation
questions.explanation: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.25-30) and Hippolytus (On Christ and Antichrist) are cited as evidence that futurist elements are ancient, even though the full modern system developed later.

questions.q: How does 'moderate' futurism differ from dispensational futurism?
options: Moderate futurists deny any future Second Coming
Moderate futurists date all of Revelation to AD 70
Moderate futurists use the day-year principle exclusively
Moderate futurists (e.g. Ladd) see the seals partly fulfilled through the church age and do not separate Israel and the church or posit a pretribulational rapture
questions.explanation: Ladd's A Commentary on the Revelation of John (1972) mixes futurism with present-age application; dispensational futurism also reads the letters to the seven churches as foreshadowing church-age eras.

questions.q: Why do some dispensational futurists regard Revelation 4:1 as significant?
options: The call 'come up here' and the absence of the word 'church' from chapters 4-19 are read as suggesting the church has been raptured
It names the Antichrist
It gives the date of Revelation
It describes the binding of Satan
questions.explanation: Critics note that John's ascent is personal and that 'saints' appear throughout chapters 4-19; dispensationalists reply that the saints in those chapters are tribulation converts.

questions.q: What do futurists consider a major strength of their approach?
options: It requires the earliest possible date for Revelation
It identifies the Pope as Antichrist
It takes the cosmic scale of Revelation's judgments and the return of Christ (Revelation 19) at face value as events not yet seen in history
It removes the need for a future Second Coming
questions.explanation: Futurists argue that worldwide judgments, a resurrection and the new creation have plainly not yet occurred; critics reply that the opening time texts (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:10) imply relevance to the first readers.

questions.q: How do futurists answer the objection that a mostly future Revelation would have been irrelevant to its first readers?
options: They concede the book was irrelevant to its first readers
They argue Revelation was written in the twentieth century
They claim the first readers lived during the tribulation
The letters to the churches addressed them directly, and the future victory of Christ gave them hope and exhortation to endure
questions.explanation: Futurists add that 'soon' may express imminence or certainty from God's perspective (2 Peter 3:8), so the book remained relevant even if fulfilment was long delayed.

questions.q: What does the idealist approach say Revelation primarily depicts?
options: The ongoing conflict between God and evil, Christ and Satan, throughout the whole church age, in symbolic form
A detailed chronology of world history
Events limited to AD 66-70
Only the last seven years before Christ returns
questions.explanation: Idealists (also called the 'spiritual' or 'symbolic' approach) read the visions as recurring patterns applicable in every generation, culminating in Christ's final victory.

questions.q: Which fourth-century North African exegete influenced Augustine toward a spiritual reading of Revelation?
options: Papias
Josephus
Tyconius
Joachim of Fiore
questions.explanation: Tyconius, a Donatist, wrote a lost commentary and a book of interpretive rules; his symbolic approach shaped Augustine's City of God and much later Western exegesis.

questions.q: Which book by William Hendriksen (1939) is a classic idealist-amillennial reading of Revelation?
options: The Blessed Hope
More Than Conquerors
Days of Vengeance
Things to Come
questions.explanation: Hendriksen divided Revelation into seven parallel sections, each running from the first coming to the second; the method is called progressive parallelism.

questions.q: What do idealists see as a strength of their approach?
options: It allows precise date-setting for Christ's return
It identifies Nero as the beast
It makes the book directly relevant to Christians in every era rather than to one generation only
It requires a literal thousand-year reign
questions.explanation: Idealists argue that apocalyptic symbols communicate theological truths about persecution, false worship and perseverance applicable in every age.

questions.q: What is a common critique of pure idealism, and the idealist reply?
options: That it detaches Revelation from concrete history; idealists reply that the symbols refer to real historical patterns and to a real final consummation
That it denies the Second Coming; they reply that it is premillennial
That it relies on a pre-70 date; they reply with Irenaeus
That it ignores Old Testament imagery; they reply it uses only Greek myths
questions.explanation: Pure idealism without a historical anchor is rare; most idealists, like Hendriksen, affirm a literal final coming, resurrection and judgment.

questions.q: Which nineteenth-century Scottish scholar is often cited as a classic idealist interpreter?
options: E. B. Elliott
J. Stuart Russell
John Walvoord
William Milligan
questions.explanation: Milligan's lectures and commentary on Revelation (1880s) argued that the book sets forth principles rather than predicting particular events.

questions.q: How does Greg Beale describe his own approach to Revelation?
options: Strict dispensational futurism
A 'redemptive-historical' or eclectic form of modified idealism that includes a future consummation
Full preterism
Strict historicism using the day-year principle
questions.explanation: Beale's NIGTC commentary (1999) holds that the visions symbolise the church-age conflict but anticipate Christ's final coming and judgment, combining idealist with some futurist and preterist elements.

questions.q: With which millennial view is idealism most often combined?
options: Dispensational premillennialism
Amillennialism
Full preterism
No millennial view has ever combined with it
questions.explanation: Reading Revelation 20 as a symbolic picture of the present age fits amillennialism naturally; Warfield's postmillennialism also drew on a broadly idealist reading of Revelation 20.

questions.q: What characterises the eclectic approach to Revelation?
options: It rejects all four classic approaches
It is identical to historicism
It applies only to Daniel
It combines elements of preterism, futurism and idealism, holding that the visions addressed first-century readers, apply to every age, and point to a future consummation
questions.explanation: Scholars such as Greg Beale, Craig Keener and Grant Osborne combine approaches, arguing each captures part of the book's purpose.

questions.q: Which reference work presents historicist, preterist, futurist and spiritual readings in parallel columns?
options: Steve Gregg's Revelation: Four Views
Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium
Scofield's Reference Bible
Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae
questions.explanation: Gregg's parallel commentary (1997; revised 2013) lets readers compare each approach verse by verse, and itself models an evenhanded, eclectic study.

questions.q: How does Craig Keener's eclectic reading treat the first readers of Revelation?
options: He holds the book was irrelevant to its first readers
He reads it as a chronology of church history
He anchors the symbols in first-century Roman Asia while applying them to later believers and to the future return of Christ
He holds it was entirely fulfilled in AD 70
questions.explanation: Keener's NIV Application Commentary on Revelation (2000) emphasises the imperial cult and persecution context while affirming a future consummation.

questions.q: What do eclectic interpreters see as the strength of their method?
options: It eliminates every interpretive disagreement
It requires only one millennial view
It avoids the Old Testament entirely
It respects the book's first-century setting, its ongoing relevance, and its genuinely future hope together
questions.explanation: Advocates argue Revelation itself combines letters to real churches, symbolic visions of recurring conflict, and prophecy of the end (Revelation 1:19 is sometimes read in this threefold way).

questions.q: What is a common critique of the eclectic approach, and the reply?
options: That it can seem arbitrary in choosing which approach to apply; eclectics reply that genre, context and Old Testament allusion guide the choice
That it denies the Second Coming; they reply it is full preterist
That it is unknown to modern scholarship; they reply it is medieval
That it requires a literal 1,260 years; they reply with the day-year principle
questions.explanation: Critics want a single controlling principle; eclectics answer that complex apocalyptic literature naturally works on several levels.

questions.q: Which verse do some interpreters use to argue Revelation has past, present and future dimensions?
options: Revelation 22:21
Revelation 13:18
Revelation 1:19 (write the things seen, the things that are, and the things to come)
Revelation 7:4
questions.explanation: Dispensationalists read the verse as an outline (chapter 1; chapters 2-3; chapters 4-22); eclectics and Beale often read it as describing the mixed temporal scope of the whole book.

questions.q: Is the eclectic approach tied to one millennial view?
options: Yes, only amillennialism
No; eclectic interpreters include amillennialists, premillennialists and postmillennialists
Yes, only dispensationalism
Yes, only full preterism
questions.explanation: Beale is amillennial, Grant Osborne is premillennial, and some postmillennialists also blend preterist and idealist readings.

questions.q: Which scholar's work on the theology of Revelation stresses its prophetic critique of Rome and its relevance as Christian prophecy?
options: John Walvoord
Max King
Richard Bauckham
Francisco Ribera
questions.explanation: Bauckham's The Theology of the Book of Revelation (1993) and The Climax of Prophecy highlight the book's Old Testament allusions and its critique of Roman power while affirming a future eschatological hope.

questions.q: What is covenant theology?
options: A framework that organises Scripture around God's covenants, often summarised as covenants of redemption, works and grace, with strong continuity between Israel and the church
A system dividing history into seven dispensations
A form of full preterism
A Roman Catholic doctrine of sacraments
questions.explanation: Covenant theology developed in the Reformed tradition (Zwingli, Bullinger, Cocceius, Witsius) and is expressed in the Westminster Confession chapter 7.

questions.q: What is the 'covenant of grace' in covenant theology?
options: A covenant made with Adam before the fall requiring perfect obedience
A covenant between the Father and the Son in eternity
A covenant made only with the church after Pentecost
God's single gracious covenant of salvation through Christ, administered differently in the Old and New Testaments
questions.explanation: The covenant of works was with Adam (Genesis 2:16-17; Romans 5:12-21), and the covenant of redemption is the intratrinitarian pact; the covenant of grace unites believers of all ages in Christ.

questions.q: How does covenant theology generally relate Israel and the church?
options: As two peoples with separate destinies
As one people of God across both testaments, with the church as the continuation and fulfilment of Israel
As unrelated entities
As identical to modern national Israel
questions.explanation: Texts such as Galatians 3:29, Galatians 6:16, Ephesians 2:11-22 and Romans 11's single olive tree are central; many covenant theologians still expect a future mass conversion of Jews (Romans 11:25-26).

questions.q: Which millennial views are most common among covenant theologians?
options: Only dispensational premillennialism
Amillennialism and postmillennialism, with a minority of historic premillennialists
Only full preterism
Only historicist premillennialism
questions.explanation: Vos, Hoekema and Riddlebarger are amillennial; Charles Hodge, Warfield, Bahnsen and Gentry are postmillennial; some Reformed thinkers, such as some Puritans, held premillennial views.

questions.q: What do Reformed Baptists (1689 Federalism) differ on with Westminster covenant theology?
options: Whether Christ will return
Whether God made any covenants at all
Whether the Bible is inspired
Whether the new covenant includes believers' children, and so whether infants should be baptised
questions.explanation: Paedobaptist covenant theology sees the sign of the covenant given to believers and their children (Genesis 17; Acts 2:39); 1689 Federalists see the new covenant as made only with the regenerate (Jeremiah 31:31-34).

questions.q: What hermeneutical principle is typical of covenant theology?
options: The New Testament's use of the Old Testament guides interpretation, so Old Testament promises are read in light of their fulfilment in Christ
Old Testament promises must be fulfilled literally to national Israel
Only the Old Testament is authoritative
Prophecy should be interpreted using the day-year principle exclusively
questions.explanation: Covenant theologians argue that Christ is the true Israel and seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:16), so promises such as the land find fulfilment in the new creation (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16).

questions.q: Which Princeton theologian is seen as a founder of Reformed biblical theology and the 'two-age' eschatological framework?
options: C. I. Scofield
Max King
Geerhardus Vos
Joseph Mede
questions.explanation: Vos's The Pauline Eschatology (1930) and Biblical Theology (1948) shaped later covenantal and amillennial thinking about the overlap of this age and the age to come.

questions.q: What criticism do dispensationalists typically raise against covenant theology, and the reply?
options: That it denies the Trinity; they reply with the Nicene Creed
That it is too recent; they reply it dates from 1909
That it rejects Romans; they reply by rejecting Galatians
That it 'spiritualises' Old Testament promises to Israel; covenant theologians reply that the New Testament itself interprets those promises as fulfilled in Christ
questions.explanation: Michael Vlach argues covenant theology is a form of 'replacement' theology; covenant theologians prefer 'fulfilment' and stress that Gentiles are grafted into Israel, not replacing it.

questions.q: What is a 'dispensation' in dispensational theology?
options: A distinct stewardship or administration of God's dealings with humanity in history (from Greek oikonomia)
A period of exactly one thousand years
A spiritual gift given to the church
A Catholic indulgence
questions.explanation: Ephesians 1:10 and 3:2 use oikonomia; Scofield described seven dispensations (innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom).

questions.q: What were Charles Ryrie's three 'sine qua non' of dispensationalism (Dispensationalism Today, 1965)?
options: Seven dispensations, a pretribulational rapture, and a pre-70 Revelation
The covenant of works, covenant of grace and covenant of redemption
A consistent distinction between Israel and the church, consistently literal (normal) interpretation, and God's glory as the ultimate purpose of history
Historicism, idealism and futurism
questions.explanation: Ryrie argued these, not the number of dispensations, define the system; progressive dispensationalists have modified the first two.

questions.q: Which order of historical development is correct?
options: Progressive, revised, classic
Classic (Darby, Scofield, Chafer), revised or normative (Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost), progressive (Blaising, Bock, Saucy)
Revised, classic, progressive
Classic, progressive, revised
questions.explanation: Classic dispensationalism sharply separated a heavenly and earthly people; revised dispensationalism moderated this; progressive dispensationalism (1990s) sees a single, progressively unfolding kingdom with an inaugurated Davidic reign.

questions.q: What do classic and revised dispensationalists mean by calling the church a 'mystery' or 'parenthesis'?
options: The church will last only a thousand years
The church is the fulfilment of all Old Testament prophecy
The church age was not revealed in Old Testament prophecy and intervenes before God resumes his programme for Israel
The church began with Abraham
questions.explanation: They cite Ephesians 3:3-6 and Colossians 1:26; progressive dispensationalists prefer to see the church as a new stage within the unfolding kingdom rather than a parenthesis.

questions.q: Which institutions and events spread dispensationalism in America?
options: The Niagara Bible Conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible, and Dallas Theological Seminary
The Westminster Assembly and Princeton Seminary
The Council of Trent and Jesuit colleges
The Synod of Dort and Leiden University
questions.explanation: The Niagara conferences (from the 1870s) promoted premillennialism; Scofield's 1909 study Bible and Lewis Sperry Chafer's founding of Dallas Theological Seminary (1924) made dispensationalism mainstream in evangelicalism.

questions.q: Why do dispensationalists say the future of national Israel is essential to their system?
options: They believe the church replaced Israel
They believe Israel's promises were fulfilled in Solomon
They hold that Israel has no future role
God's unconditional covenant promises to Abraham and David, including land and kingdom, must be fulfilled to ethnic Israel
questions.explanation: Michael Vlach (Has the Church Replaced Israel?) argues the New Testament reaffirms Israel's restoration (Matthew 19:28; Acts 1:6; Romans 11:26-29).

questions.q: What does 'literal' or 'normal' interpretation mean in dispensationalism?
options: Taking every image in Revelation as physically literal
Reading texts according to their ordinary grammatical-historical sense, recognising figures of speech, and applying this consistently to prophecy
Reading the Old Testament only through the New
Ignoring historical context
questions.explanation: Ryrie and others argued that prophecy should be read like the rest of Scripture; critics say the New Testament's own use of the Old models typological fulfilment.

questions.q: What critique of dispensationalism concerns history, and how do proponents respond?
options: That it originated in AD 70; they reply it is 1,000 years old
That its pretribulational rapture appeared only in the nineteenth century; proponents reply that truth is judged by Scripture, not age, and point to earlier hints of the idea
That it was invented by Augustine; they reply it was Origen
That it denies Romans 11; they reply by rejecting it
questions.explanation: Critics trace the pretrib rapture to Darby in the 1830s; Thomas Ice and others cite earlier writers such as Pseudo-Ephraem and Morgan Edwards as partial anticipations, though how close these are is disputed.

questions.q: What is progressive covenantalism?
options: A new form of full preterism
A Roman Catholic doctrine of tradition
A form of historicism
A framework that traces the unfolding of God's covenants through Scripture to their fulfilment in Christ, positioned between covenant theology and dispensationalism
questions.explanation: Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum's Kingdom through Covenant (2012; 2nd ed. 2018) is the defining work; 'progressive' refers to the progressive revelation of God's plan through the biblical covenants.

questions.q: How does progressive covenantalism differ from Westminster covenant theology?
options: It holds the new covenant community consists of regenerate believers, so it supports believer's baptism, and it emphasises the distinct biblical covenants rather than a single 'covenant of grace' framework
It rejects any covenant with Adam
It teaches two peoples of God
It requires infant baptism
questions.explanation: Wellum and Gentry affirm a covenant with creation/Adam, then Noah, Abraham, Israel (Moses), David and the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34).

questions.q: How does progressive covenantalism differ from dispensationalism?
options: It holds a pretribulational rapture
It denies any typology in Scripture
It sees Christ as the fulfilment of Israel and the land promise as typologically expanding to the new creation, rather than requiring a separate future for national Israel
It teaches the church replaced Israel through supersession
questions.explanation: Proponents prefer 'fulfilment' language and argue from Romans 4:13 (Abraham as heir of the world) and Hebrews 11:10-16 that the land promise expands in Christ.

questions.q: What role does typology play in progressive covenantalism?
options: Types are rejected as allegory
Types are fulfilled only in national Israel
Types replace the literal meaning entirely
Types escalate as they move through the covenants and find their fulfilment in Christ
questions.explanation: Wellum stresses that persons, events and institutions (e.g. Adam, David, temple) point forward with increasing intensity to Christ (Romans 5:14; Hebrews 8:5).

questions.q: Which millennial views are most common among progressive covenantalists?
options: Amillennialism, with some historic premillennialists
Only dispensational premillennialism
Only full preterism
Only historicist postmillennialism
questions.explanation: Wellum leans amillennial, while the framework does not require a single millennial view; it typically rejects dispensational distinctives such as a future millennial temple with sacrifices.

questions.q: How does progressive covenantalism relate to 'New Covenant Theology'?
options: They are identical names for covenant theology
New Covenant Theology is a form of dispensationalism
They are closely related, both stressing the newness of the new covenant, but progressive covenantalism is a distinct articulation with its own emphases
They have no connection
questions.explanation: New Covenant Theology (e.g. Tom Wells and Fred Zaspel) shares concerns about Mosaic law and the new covenant; progressive covenantalism developed through Gentry, Wellum and contributors to Progressive Covenantalism (2016).

questions.q: What is a common critique of progressive covenantalism, and the response?
options: That it denies Christ's return; they reply it is premillennial

Covenant theologians say it undervalues the unity of the covenant of grace and the place of children; proponents reply that Scripture's covenants are better handled individually and the new covenant is distinctively regenerate
That it is from the 1600s; they reply it is from 2012
That it rejects all typology; they reply it is allegorical
questions.explanation: The debate centres on texts such as Jeremiah 31:34 ('they shall all know me') and Hebrews 8; paedobaptists stress continuity of the household principle.

questions.q: How does progressive covenantalism view the future of ethnic Israel?
options: Israel has a separate millennial programme with temple sacrifices
Ethnic Israel will never come to faith
Many hold Romans 11 may anticipate a future turning of ethnic Jews to Christ, but within one people of God rather than as a separate programme
National Israel is identical with the church
questions.explanation: Proponents argue that all promises to Israel find their 'yes' in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20) and are shared by Jew and Gentile together.

questions.q: Which verse does the Spiritual Understanding treat as the governing statement of the whole book?
options: Revelation 1:1, 'the revelation of Jesus Christ'
Revelation 13:18, the number of the beast
Revelation 20:2, the thousand years
Revelation 22:18, the warning not to add to the book
questions.explanation: Proponents read the book as the unveiling of a Person: each chapter should reveal Christ and what he accomplished at the cross.

questions.q: What image is described as the key that opens the book?
options: The great red dragon
The Lamb standing as though slain at the centre of the throne
The woman clothed with the sun
The beast from the sea
questions.explanation: Revelation 5:5-6: the Lion of Judah conquers as the slain Lamb, so the cross is the lens for every vision.

questions.q: In this reading, what do the forehead and the hand usually signify?
options: Political and military power
Jewish and Gentile believers
The mind (thinking) and one's doing (works)
Heaven and earth
questions.explanation: Drawing on Deuteronomy 6:8, the mark on forehead or hand is a mindset and a way of living; the Father's name on the forehead (Revelation 14:1) is a renewed mind and identity.

questions.q: How does the view typically interpret 666?
options: A barcode or microchip
The number of humanity striving in its own effort, short of God's seventh-day rest
The date of the Antichrist's rise
The number of years until the end
questions.explanation: Six is read as humanity's number (made on the sixth day), falling short of seven, God's completed rest (Genesis 2:2; Hebrews 4:9-10).

questions.q: What is the 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:5-6 in the Spiritual Understanding?
options: A bodily resurrection before the millennium
The rapture of the church
The new birth: being raised with Christ into union with him
The revival of Israel
questions.explanation: The view follows the Augustinian reading (Ephesians 2:5-6; John 5:24-25): those born again already reign with Christ.

questions.q: Which pair of 'two women' structures the book's contrasts in this view?
options: Eve and Mary
Jezebel and Lydia
The harlot (Babylon) and the Bride (the New Jerusalem)
Sarah and Hagar only
questions.explanation: The harlot of Revelation 17 represents a religion of mixture and self-effort; the Bride of Revelation 21 is the people of God in union with Christ, a city coming down from heaven.

questions.q: On whom or what do Revelation's judgments mainly fall, according to this reading?
options: On believers who lack enough faith
On the old order, sin, death and the accuser
Only on the nation of Israel
On the physical earth alone
questions.explanation: Reading through the finished work ('It is finished', 'It is done'), proponents see the judgments as the end of what opposes life, so believers read from victory, not toward fear.

questions.q: Which is a common critique of the Spiritual Understanding?
options: It is too literal
It sets too many dates
It can allegorise the symbols away from their first-century setting and underplay the future hope
It ignores the Lamb
questions.explanation: Critics see a risk of subjective keys and a weakened future eschatology; proponents answer that the historical setting is the first layer, the keys come from Scripture's own usage, and Christ's appearing is affirmed.
